current_answer: Texas just added a real AI-related hiring warning: a Dallas Fed analysis finds fewer online postings in more automatable occupations after ChatGPT, including an estimated 2.6% aggregate effect on Texas Lightcast postings in 2025. That is not a layoff count, a national result or a clean adoption experiment. A broader U.S. posting analysis still finds little distinct AI-driven decline, while U.S. entry-level studies and a Norwegian null result point in different directions. The evidence now says the risk is concentrated, regional and unresolved—not imaginary, but not a universal verdict about your job.

catalogue_card.question: Did AI cut hiring in Texas?
catalogue_card.text: A Texas posting study finds a real pullback in more-automatable work. It is a regional warning, not proof that AI eliminated jobs everywhere.

summary: A Dallas Fed analysis of millions of Texas Lightcast online job postings finds that postings for more generative-AI-automatable positions were about 8% lower relative to less-exposed positions by 2025 Q1; the authors calculate a 2.6% aggregate Texas posting effect in 2025.
A balanced panel of incumbent Texas firms shows a similar 8–9% posting pullback by early 2026, so the result is not explained only by new firms or firm exits in the authors’ data.
The Texas measure is based on occupational tasks associated with actual Claude use, but it does not observe an employer’s AI rollout. It measures online ads, not hires, employment, wages or layoffs.

A broad U.S. Federal Reserve posting analysis still finds little indication of a distinct AI-driven decline. The regional split could reflect geography, timing, method or exposure measurement; it is not a national verdict.

Three U.S. exposure studies still report weaker early-career hiring, employment or initial earnings, while Norwegian records find no robust young-worker displacement. Those results remain different populations and designs, not a common causal estimate.
uncertainty: The Texas study measures online job postings and an occupational automation-exposure score, not realized hires, employment, layoffs or firm-level AI adoption.
Texas and broad U.S. posting analyses differ in geography, period, exposure metric and specification, so their contrast does not identify the cause of the split.
The U.S. early-career findings are exposure-based, not observed-adoption experiments. Remote work, education, pre-trends, other shocks and sample selection remain live attribution problems.
No current study can tell a reader whether their own job will be lost to AI.
freshness_note: Updated 17 September 2026 after a Texas analysis found an exposure-linked pullback in online postings. We will revise when comparable work applies the same method across regions, observes adoption and follows postings through to hiring, employment and pay.
